title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
dek: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
why: This episode gets the ownership of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, but staged by Lenin with Stalin performing on it. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.
who: Listeners interested in the origins of the Soviet system and how power actually operates; founders and managers who want to understand how ‘architecture’ and ‘the individual’ divide the labour.
skip: The two minutes of ads at the start and the farewell at the end are skippable; the audio-drama trailer dropped in the middle (roughly 21:55-22:56) has nothing to do with this episode.

points.h: In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
points.body: The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a terrible orator and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

points.h: Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
points.body: During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia against the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was in 1941 for Churchill to ally with Stalin — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

points.h: The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
points.body: Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system all down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this is a complete misreading of Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

points.h: Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
points.body: Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. It is said his intention was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won it decisively. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

points.h: Stalin threatened to resign whenever he was unhappy
points.body: Giles recounts a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly, for instance when he wasn't authorised at Tsaritsyn to liquidate Trotsky, he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, his work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than stay on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew tired of reading it, and then said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes this in the reader's mind: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

points.h: Nobody thought the General Secretary's job was worth having
points.body: In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

points.h: Stalin's apology letter: says sorry without admitting fault
points.body: Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was enraged, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really did offend her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

points.h: If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
points.body: Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin had gone after Lenin on his way up. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining the fluids and removing the organs, and the heart was never found again.
